topic.name: Mebendazole
topic.seo_title: Mebendazole Cancer Research - Latest Studies & Findings | Your Cancer Breakthroughs
topic.seo_description: Explore mebendazole's anti-cancer potential in off-label cancer research. Latest peer-reviewed studies, mechanisms, and clinical developments for patients.
topic.seo_intro:
Mebendazole is an anthelmintic medication traditionally used to treat parasitic worm infections in humans. In recent years, researchers have discovered that this well-established drug demonstrates promising anti-cancer activity in laboratory and preclinical studies. Scientists have identified multiple mechanisms through which mebendazole may interfere with cancer cell growth and survival, including effects on microtubule dynamics and cellular energy production. This unexpected therapeutic potential has generated significant interest in the oncology research community, leading to investigations into whether mebendazole could be repurposed as an off-label cancer treatment.

The study of mebendazole as an anti-cancer agent represents an important example of drug repurposing in cancer research. Because mebendazole has been safely used in clinical practice for decades with a well-understood safety profile, it presents a unique opportunity for rapid translation from laboratory findings to clinical evaluation. Several research groups worldwide are actively investigating its efficacy against various cancer types, though it is important to note that clinical evidence in human cancer patients remains limited at this stage. The mechanisms of action continue to be elucidated through ongoing molecular and cellular research.

This page compiles the latest peer-reviewed research on mebendazole's anti-cancer properties, clinical considerations, and ongoing studies. Whether you are a patient, caregiver, healthcare provider, or researcher seeking current information about this off-label medication in cancer treatment, the articles below represent the most recent scientific findings available. We encourage you to discuss any information found here with your oncology team before making any healthcare decisions.

articles.title: MCL1 inhibition to enhance the efficacy of MYB targeting in pediatric acute myeloid leukemia.
articles.hook: Mebendazole plus MCL1 inhibition improves pediatric acute myeloid leukemia outcomes
articles.summary: Combining MCL1 inhibition with mebendazole—which targets MYB—significantly improves treatment of pediatric acute myeloid leukemia without chemotherapy toxicity.

articles.title: From anthelmintic to neuro-oncology: A systematic review of mebendazole repurposing for brain tumour therapy.
articles.hook: Mebendazole inhibits glioblastoma growth through microtubule disruption
articles.summary: Mebendazole, an existing anti-parasite drug, shows promise against brain tumors through multiple cancer-fighting mechanisms and effective brain penetration.

articles.title: USP5 regulates purine metabolism and represents a therapeutic target in esophageal cancer.
articles.summary: USP5 protein drives esophageal cancer growth by boosting guanine production; blocking it with mebendazole improves chemotherapy effectiveness.

articles.title: Repurposing mebendazole to reprogram oncogenic and tumor-suppressor networks: Multi-cancer insights from ENOX2, MMP2, RASSF1A, WFDC10A and METTL7A.
articles.summary: Mebendazole, a common antiparasitic drug, shows promise in fighting multiple cancer types by altering key cancer-related genes.

articles.title: Mebendazole impairs the expression and function of enzymes in nucleotide metabolism pathways, leading to Selective Cytotoxicity, Cell Cycle Arrest, and Damage to Cell Morphology in Gastric Cancer.
articles.hook: Mebendazole inhibits nucleotide metabolism enzymes in gastric cancer cells
articles.summary: Mebendazole blocks nucleotide-making enzymes in gastric cancer cells, stopping their growth while sparing healthy cells.

articles.title: Efficacy of mebendazole in the spontaneous NZBxNZWF1 animal model of systemic lupus erythematosus.
articles.summary: Mebendazole treatment in lupus-prone mice reduced disease severity by decreasing protein in urine, antibody levels, and kidney damage.
